final_diagnosis.text: Long-acting anticoagulant rodenticide (brodifacoum) poisoning, most likely from eating rodents or other animals bought at a street market in China, causing an acquired vitamin K-dependent coagulopathy with gum and nose bleeding and haematuria

final_dx.text: Long-acting anticoagulant rodenticide (brodifacoum) poisoning, most likely from eating rodents or other animals bought at a street market in China, causing an acquired vitamin K-dependent coagulopathy with gum and nose bleeding and haematuria

secondary_findings: Anaemia (haemoglobin 72 g/L) from two weeks of mucosal bleeding and haematuria
Poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (raised glucose and HbA1c, glycosuria)
Chronic hepatitis B, suppressed on tenofovir, without cirrhosis: not the cause of the coagulopathy (factor V and fibrinogen normal)
accepted_differential: Vitamin K deficiency from poor diet or malabsorption
Coagulopathy of liver disease (chronic hepatitis B)
Acquired haemophilia or another acquired factor inhibitor
Congenital factor deficiency or von Willebrand disease
Deliberate self-poisoning or poisoning by another person
Haemorrhagic fever with renal involvement after travel (for example dengue, leptospirosis)
red_herrings: alcohol at a party several weeks earlier
upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and dental referral
key_discriminators: PT and APTT both 112 s with an unmeasurable INR
factors II, VII, IX and X very low with factor V normal
partial and unstable response to 10 mg doses of vitamin K
no anticoagulant medicine in the home
rodents eaten at a street market abroad
treatment_given: Intravenous vitamin K 10 mg: four doses over 48 hours, then 13 more doses during the admission; bleeding stopped, APTT normalised and the INR fell to 2.04 at discharge. Discharged on oral vitamin K 100 mg daily with haematology follow-up for INR monitoring.
outcome: INR labile between 1.00 and 1.91 over the next three months; 0.94 four months after discharge on oral vitamin K 100 mg daily. No further bleeding.

must_do.text: Give vitamin K promptly (intravenously while bleeding) for bleeding with a markedly prolonged PT and APTT
Define the defect: vitamin K-dependent factor assays (II, VII, IX, X) with factor V as the control, or at least a mixing study
Ask about anticoagulant medicines and rat poison at home and at work
Send an anticoagulant rodenticide panel when no warfarin exposure explains a vitamin K-dependent factor deficiency
Take a detailed travel and dietary history, including unusual foods eaten abroad
Plan months of high-dose oral vitamin K with regular INR checks after discharge
Involve haematology in the work-up and long-term follow-up

must_not_do.text: Treat the bleeding with tranexamic acid alone, without vitamin K
Discharge without long-term high-dose vitamin K once the INR first improves (long-acting rodenticides persist for months)
Order a liver or kidney biopsy while the coagulopathy is uncorrected
Start anticoagulant or antiplatelet drugs, including pharmacological thromboprophylaxis
Conclude deliberate self-poisoning without first taking a full dietary and travel history

diagnosis_rubric_anchors.5: Long-acting anticoagulant rodenticide poisoning, with eating animals bought at a street market abroad identified as the likely source
diagnosis_rubric_anchors.4: Long-acting anticoagulant rodenticide poisoning, source not identified
diagnosis_rubric_anchors.3: Vitamin K deficiency coagulopathy without naming a long-acting anticoagulant
diagnosis_rubric_anchors.2: Coagulopathy of liver disease, DIC, acquired haemophilia, warfarin over-anticoagulation or deliberate self-poisoning as the final diagnosis
diagnosis_rubric_anchors.1: Unrelated diagnosis, or one that would lead to harm

teaching_points: A prolonged PT and APTT with normal platelets, fibrinogen and D-dimer, and low factors II, VII, IX and X with a normal factor V, is the signature of vitamin K deficiency or antagonism rather than liver disease or DIC.
When no warfarin is involved, a long-acting anticoagulant rodenticide is the leading cause; test for it and ask again about exposure, including food.
Long-acting rodenticides persist for months: standard vitamin K doses give an incomplete, unstable response, and treatment needs high-dose oral vitamin K for months with INR monitoring.
Rodenticides accumulate in the food chain: eating rodents, or animals that prey on them, is a possible route of exposure.
